summary: Defines Concise SWID tags, a compact representation of software identification tags suited to devices with limited network and storage capacity. It keeps similar semantics to ISO/IEC 19770-2 SWID tags and adds some new ones.

plainLanguage.summary: A label that says what software is installed, written in a very small format that tiny devices can handle.

questions: how to identify software on iot devices
what are the types of coswid tags
subtitle: A compact binary form of software identification tags, built for devices with little network and storage capacity.

tldr.problem: XML-based SWID tags describe installed software well, but tags with many optional fields can be too large for constrained devices and networks.
tldr.mechanism: CoSWID defines the same kind of tag as a CBOR map described in CDDL, replacing human-readable labels with small integer indices, and signs tags with COSE.
tldr.outcome: CoSWID tags cut the size of the tag scaffolding to 10 percent or less, while supporting the same uses such as inventory, vulnerability assessment and remote attestation.

today: RFC 9393 is a Proposed Standard from June 2023. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a Concise SWID Tag
sections.content:
SWID tags, defined in ISO/IEC 19770-2:2015, are XML records that identify and describe a specific release of software, a patch, or an installation bundle. The RFC calls these software components. Each release has its own tag. Tags support software inventory management, vulnerability assessment and remote attestation.

A tag with only required fields might be a few hundred bytes, but one with many optional fields can be many orders of magnitude larger. CoSWID uses the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) from RFC 8949 to reduce this. The scaffolding takes 10 percent or less of the size, and early experiments saw a 50 to 85 percent reduction in generic usage scenarios. Values such as strings are often unchanged, so the saving depends on the application.

SWID and CoSWID are intended to share a common implicit information model, but the RFC does not define that model or a mapping between the two formats, since different groups maintain the specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Tags written in the old format can be long, like a letter full of fancy words. CoSWID writes the same facts in a short code, like a text message.

sections.title: The Four Tag Types and the Software Lifecycle
sections.content:
Like SWID, CoSWID defines four kinds of tag, tied to the software lifecycle. A primary tag describes an installed software component and is installed along with it. A patch tag describes an installed patch. A corpus tag describes installable software in its pre-installation state, for example an installer, and is not deployed on the target system. A supplemental tag adds information to another tag, so tools and users can record their own metadata without changing tags made by the software provider.

When software is installed, its tag is installed; when it is upgraded, new primary and supplemental tags replace the old ones; when it is removed, its tags are removed. The type is set by the corpus, patch and supplemental items, and the first matching rule decides: primary if all three are false, then supplemental, then corpus, then patch. A tag for a patch installer with both corpus and patch true is a corpus tag.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of labels on a toy: one on the box before you open it, one on the toy itself, one for a repair, and one with your own notes.

sections.title: How CoSWID Is Encoded
sections.content:
The structure is described in the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) from RFC 8610. CamelCase names from the XML schema become hyphenated names, for example resource-collection, and the 57 text labels of the vocabulary are mapped to integer indices, which saves space. New constructs get new indices, so no explicit CoSWID version is needed. Text strings are UTF-8 and MUST follow the Net-Unicode definition from RFC 5198.

Many values are an integer label with text escape: the integer comes from an IANA registry, and text is meant only for private use. Encoders SHOULD NOT use registered names as strings, and a decoder MUST accept unknown strings and ignore the construct. A pattern called one-or-more allows either a single value or an array of two or more, so a single value needs no array markers.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing long words like name and version, CoSWID uses little numbers as nicknames, and both sides keep the same nickname list.

sections.title: The Tag Structure
sections.content:
The root is the concise-swid-tag map. It requires a tag-id, a tag-version, a software-name and at least one entity. The tag-id is a 16-byte binary string or text and MUST be globally unique. If it is binary it MUST be a valid UUID from RFC 4122, and a text value MUST NOT contain two underscores in a row. A new tag-version MUST be greater than the old one, which lets a producer correct a tag without changing the software.

Optional items include software-version, version-scheme, link, software-meta, and either payload (files and processes shipped or installed, supplied by an external entity) or evidence (what a discovery tool found on an endpoint). Those two are mutually exclusive.

Each entity names an organization and its role. Every tag MUST have an entity with the tag-creator role, and SHOULD have a software-creator entity if known. A link uses rel values such as patches or requires and an href that may use the swid: scheme to name another tag by its tag-id. Co-constraints include that patch and supplemental MUST NOT both be true, and a patch tag MUST have a link with rel patches.
sections.plainLanguage: Every tag has an ID number, a name, and who made it. It can also point to related tags and list the files that belong to the program.

sections.title: Extension Points and Registries
sections.content:
CoSWID adds two things beyond SWID: explicit types for some attributes that SWID leaves as generic any-attributes, and CDDL sockets that allow extensions. The RFC defines sockets for the root map and for entity, link, software-meta, resource-collection, file, directory, process, resource, payload and evidence entries, plus enumeration sockets for version scheme, role, ownership, rel and use.

Section 6 of the RFC sets up six new IANA registries, including "CoSWID Items", so that extensions get well-known index values, and adds new values to five other registries. It registers the application/swid+cbor media type, CoAP Content-Format 258 and CBOR tag 1398229316. The swid and swidpath scheme names are registered as provisional because they are interpreted in a local context rather than as global URI schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag format has built-in slots for new fields, and a public list keeps everyone's new field numbers from clashing.

sections.title: Signing and Tagging
sections.content:
Signing follows CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) from RFC 9052. A CoSWID MUST be wrapped in a COSE signature structure, either COSE_Sign1 with a single signature that MUST be made by the tag creator, or COSE_Sign with several signatures, one of which MUST come from the tag creator. The protected header uses the content type application/swid+cbor. A COSE countersignature MAY be added, which lets a second party prove a signature existed at a given time.

CoSWID tags SHOULD carry the CoSWID CBOR tag, 1398229316. If a signed tag is tagged, the CoSWID CBOR tag goes before the COSE envelope, and other CBOR tags MUST NOT be used on a CoSWID item.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is like a wax seal on a letter. If someone changes the letter, the seal shows it was tampered with.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
A validated signature shows that a tag is unchanged since signing, but not that its statements are true: anyone can sign claims. Linking a signing key to the software provider is left to local policy. Tags have no expiry, so a consumer should check for updated tag versions by more than one means. A collection of tags is not guaranteed to be a complete or accurate inventory, since tags can be added or removed without matching the software.

Tag contents are meant to be public, so tag authors are advised not to put private license keys in entitlement-key. Reports of an endpoint's tags can reveal its attack surface and, per the privacy section, can hint at personal matters, so they should be protected in transit and at rest. Tags can also be built with link loops or malicious content, so implementations should sanitize input, detect loops and verify signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of what is on your computer is useful to helpers but also to bad guys, so keep that list private and be careful with tags from strangers.
